titlePart.seg:
Notes on Some Receipts from Soknopaiou Nesos
∗ This article was written in the course of project “500 Years of Writing and Literacy in the Fayum (2nd Century BCE to 3rd Century CE): Greek Writing Practices in Soknopaiou Nesos” (Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft – Project number 536675991). I am grateful to W. Graham Claytor and Nikolaos Gonis for their comments and suggestions. ∗

div.p:
In what follows, I present a series of textual corrections and palaeographical and prosopographical notes on some tax and rent receipts from Soknopaiou Nesos dating from the mid-first to the early third century, alongside a re-edition (5).
All dates are CE. Unless otherwise noted, the provenance of the papyri is Soknopaiou Nesos. In addition to a handful of novel prosopographical observations on the taxpayers (2, 6) and the identification of a previously unknown tax collector (3), the dossiers of already known tax collectors are expanded (1, 4–7, 10), while the nature of the payments recorded is clarified in a few instances (1, 7–9).

P.Louvre 1 24 is a receipt from 52/3, the decipherment of which has been severely hindered by a highly cursive and challenging handwriting, as well as by material damage across its surface. In particular, the identities of the tax collectors and taxpayer, as well as the nature of the tax, have remained uncertain. The relevant information is contained in ll. 3–5, which were read as follows: δι[α]γ[έ]γ(ραφεν) ̣ ̣τη | καὶ̣ μ̣ε̣τ̣[ό]χ(οις) Παπάις Πετεχόν(τος) αρ ̣ι ̣|σ̣ ̣ ̣ι̣( ) ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣.

A closer examination of the passage on the plate (Taf. 23) allows most of these textual difficulties to be resolved.
A low-resolution image is also available online, but it is of little help. Starting with the name of the tax collector, the editor proposed reading it as either Π̣α̣τη( ) or Π̣ω̣τη( ), noting that “allerdings irritiert die Schleife am Beginn der Querhaste” (l. 3 n.). In fact, what was taken as the left part of a pi is the abbreviation for δι(ά), whose overstroke ligatures into a sigma. The name Σωτη(ρίχου) can be read. At the beginning of l. 4, there is no mention of “associates”; rather, a colleague with the same name appears: καὶ Σωτη̣(ρίχου). After that, a chi, already recognized by the editor, is topped by a horizontal stroke indicating an abbreviation. This is to be resolved as χ(ειριστῶν), the expected title for tax collectors during this period.
On the cheiristai, see Hagedorn, BGU 20, pp. 93–97.

The taxpayer presents greater difficulties. As the editor observed, “scheint unklar, wo sein (Vaters)name endet und etwas Neues beginnt.” The beginning of l. 5 is undoubtedly occupied by the name of the tax: the cross above the line seen by the editor is a raised tau, and the whole sequence should be read as συ̣ν̣τ(αξίμου) Σοκ(νοπαίου) Ν̣ή(σου). Since no additional information is expected between the taxpayer’s identifying details and the tax name, I have considered reading Ἀρείο̣υ̣ after Πετεχόν(τος) in l. 4. However, the shape of the supposed upsilon is not entirely convincing, and one can understand why the editor saw a nu after the iota (l. 4 n.); moreover, papponyms are uncommon in this period. A professional designation would in principle also be possible; see e.g. P.Tebt. 2 349.3 (Tebtynis, 28).

One of the two Soterichoi of P.Louvre 1 24 may be the same as the cheiristes of P.Gen. 2 90.2 (with PN correction by D. Hagedorn), dated to 36, but both tax collectors recur in P.Berl.Cohen 1. This papyrus, also published in Cohen 2007, contains a replacement for a lost syntaximon receipt, dated after November 17, 41 (κ ̣ should be read instead of κ in l. 3) and written in a hand very similar to, if not identical with, that of P.Louvre 1 24. In ll. 3–4, the editor read διαγέγ(ραπται) διὰ Διωδώδ(ου) (l. Διοδότου) | [ ̣ ̣]μ[ ±3 ] ̣ς Παπάϊτο(ς) Ἀμ̣ά̣σ̣ι(ος) and noted that “the beginning of line 4 is occupied by the taxpayer’s name, or actually what was left of it, reserving no space for any title for Diodotus.” Apart from the obvious resolution διαγέγ(ραφε), what follows can now be read and restored as δι(ὰ) Σωτη(ρίχου) καὶ Σωτ̣η̣(ρίχου) | [χ(ειριστῶν)].

The few extant traces of the taxpayer’s name may be transcribed as Ε ̣[ ̣] ̣ ̣ς (Ἕκ̣[υ]σ̣ι̣ς?), while what follows the patronymic remains uncertain in this case as well. Ἀμ̣ά̣σ̣ι(ος) does not seem to be possible. The raised letter appears to be eta (cf. Σωτη(ρίχου), l. 3), but I have not been able to provide a satisfactory reading of the name.

The omission of (δραχμάς) in the sequence ἀργ(υρίου) (δραχμὰς) δεκαδύο in l. 8, correctly printed in Cohen 2007: 113, was already noted by Mitthof 2008: 268. To this adjustment, I add two further minor corrections:

ll. 4–5: συντ(άξιμον) κ̣[ώμ(ης)] | [Σοκν]οπ(αίου) Νή̣σο[υ] τοῦ αὐτοῦ (ἔτους) → συντ(αξίμου) | [Σ]οκ̣(νοπαίου) Νή̣σο(υ) τοῦ αὐτο(ῦ) (ἔτους). At the beginning of l. 5, [Σ]οκ̣(νοπαίου) is preferable to [Σοκν]οπ(αίου) on account of the width of the lacuna and the shape of the raised letter, which does not match a pi;
ll. 7–8: τὸ̣ α̣ὐτὸ σύμ|[βολον → αὐτὸ τὸ σύμ|[βολον.

The text of this receipt, originally published by Poethke and Sijpesteijn 1984: 48–49, has been significantly improved by D. Hagedorn and F. Reiter.
Corrections to ll. 2–4 by Hagedorn (and Reiter per litt.), BGU 20, p. 105 n. 24. One further refinement concerns the reading of the taxpayer’s name. In l. 3, where Hagedorn and Reiter read Παπεῖτος (l. Παπεῖς) ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣( ) τοῦ Παπεῖτος | μη(τρὸς) Θασῆτος, I see Πάπεις Π̣[ά]πειτ(ος) το(ῦ) Πάπειτος.

A certain Stotoetis son of Papeis, grandson of Papeis, mother Thases, appears in SB 16 12300.4 (111) as performing the five-day work on the Epagathian canal and in SB 16 12294.3–4 (112) as a taxpayer. The first editors and Hagedorn and Reiter hypothesized that this Stotoetis was a family member of the taxpayer in SB 16 12796. It can now be confirmed that they were brothers.

This receipt for syntaximon and merismoi is one of the earliest in Soknopaiou Nesos to be issued by praktores argyrikon. In ll. 2–3, after the indication of the accounting period, the editor read διέγρα(ψε) ̣ ̣ ̣] ̣ταμο̣υ̣η̣λ( ) καὶ μετ̣ό̣χ(οις) | πράκ(τορσιν) ἀργ(υρικῶν) Σ̣[οκ(νοπαίου) Νήσ(ου), but ̣ταμο̣υ̣η̣λ( ) does not match any name. The online image clearly shows that the correct reading is διέγρα(ψε)] δι(ὰ) Ἀκουσιλ(άου) καὶ μετόχ(ων) | πρακ(τόρων) ἀργ(υρικῶν). A blank space would have preceded διέγρα(ψε) in the lacuna.

One would expect the village indication to follow the name of the tax rather than the title of the tax collectors in this period: cf. e.g. SB 16 12294.4 or P.Fay. 54.6 (Euhemeria, 118). Moreover, if it is restored in the lacuna in l. 3, there is very little space left for the taxpayer’s identifying details. In the ed. pr., these were read as Στο]τοῆτ(ις) Σατα̣β̣[ο](ῦτος) [μη(τρὸς) Ταμ]ύσθ(ας), but the absence of the papponym would be unusual in this period. Additionally, the transcription does not account for the ink trace visible after Στο]τοητ( ): this may belong to a cursive tau ligatured to an omicron, which is now lost in the lacuna. As for l. 4, the ed. pr. reads ἐννεακαιδεκάτου (ἔτους) (δραχμὰς) ὀκτώ, but there seems to be something more on the papyrus. I interpret the end of the ordinal number as written with Verschleifung and ligatured to an L-shaped symbol, of which only the lower part survives. This is followed, as I see it, by a sigma, two further traces and a sinusoid. On this basis, I would read the passage as follows: Σ[ ± 7 Στ]ο̣τοήτ(εως) τ̣[ο(ῦ)] Σατα̣β̣[οῦ]τ̣(ος) [μη(τρὸς) Ταμ]ύσθ(ας) συντ(αξίμου) | ἐννεακαιδεκάτου (ἔτους) Σο̣κ̣(νοπαίου Νήσου) (δραχμὰς?) ὀ̣κτώ.
For the extreme abbreviation Σοκ(νοπαίου Νήσου), cf. e.g. BGU 3 762.1 (163).

This papyrus contains two receipts for the camel tax, dated to 148 and 149, written by two different scribes. While only the right-hand part of the second receipt survives, the first one has been entirely reconstructed thanks to the join with a Berlin fragment, originally published as BGU 15 2542 (see P.Brookl., Pl. X for the join). In l. 5 of this text, the editor tentatively read [δι’] Ἑ̣ρμί̣ω̣ν̣[ος καὶ μετόχ(ων) πρακ(τόρων)], which was retained in P.Brookl. 14 with no changes except that rho and mu were also dotted, and the second part of the line was placed outside the brackets. However, the name Hermion is not otherwise attested in Soknopaiou Nesos, while a Charmion appears as a tax collector in office between 149 and 150 in SB 24 16185 (149–151). In fact, this name should be read in P.Brookl. 14 as well. In the lacuna at the beginning of the line, there is room for nothing more than chi, whose ascending diagonal is partly visible. The dative formula Χ̣αρμίων̣ι̣ κ̣α̣ὶ̣ μ̣ετόχ(οις) πράκ(τορσι) can therefore be read.

A minor improvement can be made in the second receipt, in l. 14. The plate allows the reading μ]έτοχοι πρακτώρ(ων) (l. μετόχων πρακτόρων) instead of μ]ετ̣όχ(ων) πρακτώρ(ων). The same error, with the nominative instead of the genitive and the spelling πρακτωρ- instead of πρακτορ-, is also found in the first receipt in SB 24 16185.3–4 and in the first receipt in P.Lond. inv. 1588a.4 (151–152; ed. Gonis 2016: 414–417), both written by the same hand as P.Brookl. 14.
On the identity of the first hand in P.Lond. inv. 1588a, the first hand in SB 24 16185 and the fourth hand in SB 16 12327 (147–149), see Gonis 2016: 414. BGU 1 214 (152) can also be assigned to the same scribe, which justifies the transcription καὶ μέτοχοι [π]ρακ[τ]ώ̣ρ(ων) (l. μετόχων πρακτόρων) instead of the ed. pr.’s καὶ μέτοχοι [π]ράκ[τ]ορ[ες] in l. 6.

The text of this receipt, originally published by Daris 1976 with a number of unresolved issues, was reprinted as SB 14 11427 with a corrected date and subsequently as P.Palau Rib. 51 with minor changes. The online image enabled me to suggest a minor correction to l. 4 (Borrelli 2026: 220 n. 19, 242). However, the decipherment of passages that the first editor was unable to read and a number of further refinements to the transcription now warrant a re-edition of the document. This makes it possible to identify both the tax collector and the taxpayer.

The tax collector, Herieus (l. 4), also issues the receipts preserved by P.Lond. 2 319 (157) and BGU 1 212 (158). The latter is written by the same scribe as P.Palau Rib. 51, who likely also wrote P.Lond. 2 319, P.Coll.Youtie 1 40 (159, on which see below §6), P.Lond. 2 323 (160), BGU 2 654 (161) and 1 219.1–8 (161). Regarding the taxpayer (l. 5), it is most likely the same weaver, Herieus son of Harpagathes, who pays the cheironaxion in P.Brux. inv. E 7908.4–5 (144; ed. Bingen 2010: 246–248) and in P.Heid. 3 238.4 (162), and who is entrusted with a girl for work or apprenticeship in BGU 3 855.4–5 (147).
An identification of the taxpayer of P.Heid. 3 238 with that of P.Brux. inv. E 7908.4–5 was suggested by Bingen 2010: 247. Incidentally, I note that there is no scribal error in P.Brux. inv. E 7908.4, where the editor read Ἁξπα̣γάθο(υ) (l. Ἁρπαγάθου). As can be seen from the plate (Fig. 3), the expected Ἁρπα̣γάθο(υ) occurs: the loop of the rho is simply open on the left. The same is true for l. 2, where Καίσαρος should be read instead of Καίσαξος (l. Καίσαρος). On BGU 3 855, see Claytor 2024: §§ 15–17.

note.p: 4. διέγρ(αψε) δι’ Ἑριέω̣[ς: διαγ(έγραπται) δι’ Ἑρμ̣ ̣[ ̣ ̣ ̣ ed. (δι’ Ερω[ ̣ ̣ ̣ SB 14 11427). The second epsilon of Ἑριέω̣[ς is so reduced as to be barely recognizable, which is not surprising in view of how Ἀντωνίνου is written in l. 3.

πρακ(τόρων) Borrelli 2026: π(ρακτόρων) κ(ώμης) ed. The first three letters are reduced to a single curved stroke. For a similar abbreviation with an additional stroke, cf. BGU 1 212.5 and 219.5: in both, I propose reading πρακ(τόρων) instead of πρ(α)κ(τόρων).
5. Ἁρπ[αγάθου]: Ἁρπ[ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣] ed. For this supplement, see above.

6. φιλ[ανθρ]ώ̣(που) κωμογρ(αμματέως): φιλ[άνθρωπο]ν κωμογρ(αμματεῖ) ed., but the lacuna is too short and the name of the tax is expected in the genitive. For the raised omega, cf. λοιπῶ(ν), l. 5. On the resolution of the abbreviation κωμογρ( ) in the genitive, see P.Jördens 22.i.1 n.
7. ἔ[τους] Σοκνοπ(αίου) Νήσ[ου]: ἔ[τους ̣ ̣ ̣ ̣] Σοκνο(παίου) ̣ ̣ ̣[ ed. Νήσ[ο(υ)], as in BGU 1 212.7, is also possible.

8. This line was left unread by the editor. In the lacuna I restore the abbreviated form ἑξ[ήκον(τα) for reasons of space, based on comparison with BGU 1 212.8. I have considered whether what follows ξ̣δ might be the surcharges. These are normally calculated at the rate of 1/16, which would amount to 4 drachmas (cf. [ ̣]δ[, l. 9). However, I cannot match what I see with προσδιαγραφόμενα in any way.
On the date, see BL 8.84. Regarding the emperor’s titulature, note that Σεβαστοῦ (l. 3) is not abbreviated but written with Verschleifung.

div.p: This receipt for camel tax is issued by a tax collector whose name in l. 3 has been almost entirely lost. Only the first two letters survive, printed as Σω̣[, though Σα̣[ was also considered (l. 3 n.). Comparison with P.Lond. 2 323 (160), BGU 2 654 (161) and 1 219.1–8 (161), all written by the same scribe as the papyrus in question, shows that the latter reading should be preferred. Σα̣[ταβοῦτος] fits the length of the lacuna; however, the designation of this man as πρεσβ(υτέρου) (l. 4) rules out identifying him with the homonymous tax collector attested in the other receipts.

Regarding the taxpayer, the editor rightly observed that “only one person seems to be mentioned in lines 4–5” (ll. 3–6 n.). The few extant traces at the beginning of l. 5 are compatible with reading the patronymic Ὥ̣ρ[ο]υ̣; for the tall upsilon, of which only the upper loop is visible in the interlinear space, cf. Νήσου in l. 6 and especially Ὥρου in P.Lond. 2 323.6. [τελέ]σ̣ματ(ος) immediately follows, with no intervening text.

Four receipts for camel tax from the late 150s and early 160s record payments by an Hekysis son of Horos (P.Lond. 2 323.6; BGU 2 654.5) and by a Pakysis son of Horos (P.Lond. 2 319.6; SPP 22 155.5–6, from 162).
On Hekysis, who is also known from several camel declarations, see Hagedorn 2018: 173–174. Pakysis is most likely the same as the Pekysis son of Horos who appears as the purchaser of a female camel in BGU 1 100.2 (January 3, 159). This points to Soknopaiou Nesos as the provenance of that papyrus. They may be brothers, and either could be the taxpayer named in P.Coll.Youtie 1 40.4–5: the lacuna at the end of l. 4 accommodates approximately 7 letters.

A minor refinement may also be proposed for the line division between ll. 5 and 6. At the end of l. 5, the editor printed δευτέρου κ (ἔτους) and calculated a lacuna of about 13 letters before Σοκ]ν̣οπ(αίου) Νήσου in the following line, which, however, appears excessively long. BL 8.84 records the correction δευτέρου καὶ | [εἰκοστοῦ (ἔτους). καί is correct, but [εἰκοστοῦ] should be supplied in the same line; in the next line, ἔτους, written out, fills the lacuna.

Between 166 and 168, a group of receipts for the dyke tax attests the activity of the praktor argyrikon Dioskoros: BGU 1 99 (August 2, 166); SB 6 9426 (August 23, 166); P.Bas. 2 23 (November 9, 166); BGU 11 2028 (July 17, 168); P.Lond. 2 337 (August 18, 168). In P.Prag. 1 58.4 (February 10, 168), his name is almost entirely restored.

With the exception of the last document, all of these papyri may be attributed to the same scribe, who also wrote SPP 22 139 (October 5, 168).
The hypothesis that BGU 1 99 and BGU 11 2028 were written by the same hand was previously suggested in BGU 11 2028.7 n., based on the shared spelling μετωχ( ). In the introduction to the edition of P.Bas. 2 23, W.G. Claytor draws attention to the similarity in format to BGU 1 99, but he argues against identifying the hands. It is true that some abbreviations differ (e.g. διά and μετ(όχων) in P.Bas. 2 23 vs. δι(ά) vs. μετώχ(ων) in BGU 1 99), but other features may point to a single scribe, such as the rendering of καί and Σοκνοπ(αίου) Νήσου, or the distinctive shape of upsilon with a connecting stroke extending to the following letter. Lines 5–7 of this papyrus were printed in the ed. pr. as διέγρ(αψε) | [ ]ο̣ρου καὶ μετόχ(οις) | [πράκτ(ορσι) ἀρ]γ(υρικῶν) κτλ. Sijpesteijn 1982: 186 n. 28 (= BL 8.487) proposed the correction ] Ὥρου καὶ μετώχ(οις) (l. μετόχοις) in l. 6, but what he read as an omega is in fact an omicron ligatured with the preceding letter. The text may therefore be restored as [δι(ὰ) Διοσ]κ̣όρου καὶ μετώχ(ων) (l. μετόχων) | [πρακ(τόρων) ἀρ]γ(υρικῶν).

This document adds to the dossier of the praktor Dioskoros and must likewise be a receipt for the dyke tax. In l. 11, where the editor transcribed ]το( ), the papyrus actually has ]ϛ, which corresponds exactly to the amount recorded in the other receipts (6 drachmas and 4 obols). On the basis of these parallels, the following text can be read instead of the ed. pr.’s μη]τ(ρὸς) Ταφι|[ώμιος ] ἑβδόμου ἔτ[ους ] | [ ]το( ) καὶ τὰ προ[σδ(ιαγραφόμενα):
[τοῦ ±3] ̣ ̣ ̣[±2] μ̣ητ(ρὸς) Ταφιώ̣(μιος)
10 [χωμάτ(ων)] τ̣οῦ ἑβδόμου ἔτ[ους]
[δρ(αχμὰς) ἓξ (τετρώβολον), (γίνονται) (δραχμαὶ)] ϛ (τετρώβολον) καὶ τὰ προσ[δ(ιαγραφόμενα)]
[συμβολ(ικά)].

As for P.Prag. 1 58.4, the tax collector’s name is almost completely abraded, but the editor noted that “l’integrazione (i.e. διὰ [Διοσκό]ρ̣ο̣υ), grazie alla data della ricevuta, è sicura” (l. 4 n.). However, inspection of the online image reveals a difficulty with the final letter. The descending stroke curves to the left, not to the right as in the other instances, and it is too long to belong to an upsilon. A raised eta is preferable from a palaeographical perspective, and a supplement [Στοτ]ο̣ή̣(τιος) is supported by comparison with P.Prag. 1 57.4. This receipt, written by the same scribe as P.Prag. 1 58 and issued by the praktor Stotoetis (whose name is written in full rather than abbreviated
Read Στοτόη̣τις (l. Στοτοήτεως) instead of Στοτοήτ(εως); the same ligature ιϲ is found in Ἄνχωφις̣ (Ἀνχῶφ(ις) ed. pr.) in l. 6. ), was dated by the editor to November 13, 166: ἔτ̣ους ἑβδό[μο]υ̣ was printed in l. 1, but the lacuna between omicron and upsilon is too short for μο. Furthermore, what was read as εβ looks more like ογ̣: for a similar omicron, closed at the top by a small thickening, cf. Οὐήρου in l. 2. The identification of gamma is complicated by the horizontal stroke on the baseline, which may be the result of a scribal correction (beta is not possible in any case). On this basis, I suggest reading the regnal year as ἔτ̣ους ὀγ̣δό[ο]υ̣, which would redate the document to November 14, 167, only a few months before P.Prag. 1 58.

This fully preserved receipt is very difficult to decipher owing to its extensive use of abbreviation and Verschleifung. Consequently, its content has largely been misinterpreted. After U. Wilcken’s revision (= BL 1.35), ll. 4–9 run as follows:
διέγρ(αψεν) Σ ̣ ̣( ) καὶ μετόχ(οις) πρά(κτορσιν) Σαταβοῦς
5 Πακύσεως καὶ Στοτοῆτις
᾽Οννώφρεως ἡγο(ύμενοι) κώμ(ης)
Σοκ(νοπαίου) Νή(σου) τὸ τέλ(ος) ὑπ(ὲρ) λα (ἔτους) ἀργ(υρίου) (δραχμὰς)
τετρακοσίας (γίνονται) (δραχμαὶ) υ
(m.2) πλήρης.

In view of the plural ἡγο(ύμενοι), the correct resolution of διεγρ( ) in l. 4 is διέγρ(αψαν), not διέγρ(αψεν). Moreover, πλήρης is part of the main text and was written by the main scribe, as in similar cases: cf. e.g. BGU 7 1587.6 (Philadelphia, 258).

Regarding the tax collector, an improvement was recently made by Iannace 2026: 195, who identified the name Σεύ(θῃ) in l. 4. This reading may appear suspect at first sight because of both the shape of the abbreviation mark — in which one might seek to read a letter — and the lack of secure attestation of the name Seuthes in Soknopaiou Nesos.
The reading of the same name in P.Aberd. inv. 13f.2 (ed. Iannace 2026: 192–195) is far from certain. However, if l. 7 is interpreted correctly (see below), the use of this semicircular form for an abbreviation mark would be idiosyncratic to the scribe. Moreover, what follows Σεύ(θῃ) on the papyrus justifies the presence of an unusual name for Soknopaiou Nesos. This is a series of indistinct wave-like strokes, after which a clear chi is visible. What Wilcken, guided by the context, interpreted as a pi is in fact an epsilon ligatured to an iota of the type seen in καί, l. 5. The raised letter following rho is an omega, not an alpha; thus, χειρω should be read. In Soknopaiou Nesos, the trade tax was not collected by the πράκτορες ἀργυρικῶν, but by the μισθωταί / ἐγλήμπτορες or the ἐπιτηρηταὶ κοπῆς τριχὸς καὶ χειρωναξίου. These tax collectors often bore names that were atypical for the village.
See Reiter 2004: 116–118, who argues that these officials could operate at district level. See p. 117 n. 31 for a list of occurrences of the farmers of this tax in Soknopaiou Nesos. In l. 4 of the present papyrus, an initial epsilon is discernible, while the sequence γλημ may be recognized in the reduced letters that follow. I therefore suggest reading ἐγλήμπτορι χειρω(ναξίου), taking ἐγλήμπτορι to be written with Verschleifung, since abbreviations are consistently marked throughout the document. For the shortened title ἐγλήμπτωρ χειρωναξίου, cf. P.Brux. inv. E 7908.3 (Bingen 2010: 246–248).

The purpose of the payment is found in l. 7, where I read τελέ(σματος) instead of Wilcken’s τὸ τέλ(ος). The abbreviation mark has the same curved shape as in l. 4, though here it extends to the baseline and is ligatured with the following letter. Deciphering what comes between τελέ(σματος) and λα (ἔτους) is not straightforward. While one can see why Wilcken read ὑπ(έρ), the preposition appears superfluous before the tax year. Assuming that the curved stroke marks an abbreviation rather than standing for the letter pi, I propose reading either τ(οῦ) or το(ῦ) (the thick dot attached to the end of tau could be an omicron; cf. Αἰλίου in l. 2); for the v-shaped tau, cf. τελέ(σματος) in the same line. Although the profession is not explicitly mentioned, it is likely that we are dealing with the trade tax on weavers, also referred to simply as a τέλεσμα in P.Grenf. 2 60.6 (194). For an example of a payment made with a two-year delay, see e.g. P.Brux. inv. E 7908.6–7 (Bingen 2010: 246–248). The high amount recorded here, namely 400 drachmas, may be explained if the hegoumenoi were acting as representatives of the village’s entire community of weavers: cf. P.Amh. 2 119 (200), discussed by Reiter 2004: 117–118.

BGU 11 2102 is a receipt for φόρος προβάτων paid by the village elders of Soknopaiou Nesos to Theoninos alias Ptol( ) and his associates, lessees of ousiac properties.
On the ousia of Theoninos, see TM Geo 2377 and below, §§. The editor printed ll. 2–3 as εἰς τ(ὸν) Θεωνε̣ίνου τοῦ καὶ Πτο̣λ̣( ) | κ̣α̣ὶ̣ τῶ[ν σ]ὺ̣ν̣ α̣ὐ̣τῷ μ̣[ι]σθ(ωτῶν) οὐσι[α]κ(ῶν) κτ[ημ(άτων?)] ̣ ̣α̅ τ̣ρ ̣[ ] ̣ ̣ and noted that “am Ende der Zeile müßte λόγον gestanden haben, was aber dort kaum gelesen werden kann; vielleicht ] ̣ ̣αλ” (l. 3 n.). The online image confirms that τό̣(ν), considered by the editor (l. 2 n.) but ultimately abandoned, should indeed be read instead of τ(όν), and that the expected λόγον is in fact written on the papyrus. Moreover, the title of Theoninos can be completed by comparison with SB 20 14396.4–7 (195), where the same lessee appears alongside a colleague. The end of l. 3 may therefore be read as κτ[η]μ̣(άτων) κ̣α̣ὶ̣ ἄλ(λων) λόγ̣ο̣(ν).

The payment is made through a certain Sotas, whose identification with his namesake in the later P.Bour. 29 (see below, §§) was considered unlikely by the editor (l. 4 n.). I suggest identifying him with the Sotas son of Ptolemaios who is listed among the village elders in P.Ryl. 2 89.4–5 (191/2) and, along with the other village elders, pays rent in SPP 22 120.3 (194–195). The text of this receipt has undergone two minor corrections,
BL 8.485 and Borrelli 2026: 242 on ll. 1 and 2 respectively. but the main issue, namely the purpose of the payment, has not yet been addressed. The editor read φόρου οὐσ(ιακοῦ) [ὑπὲρ] τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἔτους in l. 4. Quite apart from the oddity of the “ousiac rent,” which is not attested elsewhere,
The phrase οὐσια(κοῦ) φό(ρου) παραδ(είσων) in P.Oxy. 12 1436.42 (Teis, 156) seems to be more specific. there are traces on the papyrus after ουϲ̅ that do not fit ὑπέρ. Immediately before τοῦ, a raised letter of which two parallel vertical strokes remain is visible: beta looks plausible (cf. πρεσβ(ύτεροι), l. 3). The preceding traces are consistent with the transcription π̣ρ̣ο̣β̣( ). I therefore suggest reading φόρου οὐσ(ιακῶν) π̣ρ̣ο̣β̣(άτων). The difficulty of an otherwise unattested formula remains. However, it is perhaps not unreasonable to assume that this is an alternative designation of the common φόρος προβάτων, which was mostly associated with imperial estates.
Note that a group of second-century receipts from Bakchias records payments ὑπὲρ οὐσιακῶν προβάτων. According to Reiter 2004: 159 n. 74, these correspond to the rent for the sheep of an ousia. In any case, the qualification as οὐσιακά may serve to distinguish these sheep from those described as δημόσια: see in particular P.Stras. 5 427.3 of 126.

As pointed out in BGU 13 2298 introd., these two receipts are written by the same hand. Both record payments of the φόρος προβάτων by the village elders of Soknopaiou Nesos for the estate formerly owned by Theoninos. Major corrections to the text of P.Bour. 29.7–8 were proposed by H. Maehler in BGU 11 2102 introd. (= BL 6.24 ), allowing its content to be fully understood. Subsequently, the edition of BGU 13 2298 led to a further improvement in l. 10 (= BL 8.68). One problem remained unresolved, however, namely the abbreviated word that opens the body of the receipt. In P.Bour. 29, it was printed as παρ(ά), and the following πρεσβ( ) was expanded into the genitive. In BGU 13 2298.5 and 10, W. Brashear read παρ(έσχον) πρεσβ(ύτεροι), noting that the same verb, “corresponding to διέγραψε, -αν in parallel receipts,” would have appeared in P.Bour. 29 as well (l. 5 n.).
The correction is recorded in BL 7.31. The online images reveal that both papyri have διέ(γραψαν): in all three instances where the same abbreviation appears, the delta merges into an extremely short iota (cf. δι(ά) in P.Bour. 29.7, with BL 6.24), which ligatures into an epsilon connected to a sinusoid.

A few further corrections to BGU 13 2298 seem to be in order. In this receipt, the payment is split over two consecutive months. As noted by the editor (l. 13 n.), the total amount of 443 drachmas and 3 obols corresponds to the sum elsewhere attested for the φόρος προβάτων. However, the editor was only able to read the name of this rent in relation to the second installment (φό(ρου) | προβ(άτων) ιϛ (ἔτους), ll. 11–12), while the purpose of the first payment remained mostly unread: in l. 7, φόρου α ̣ ̣[ ̣ ̣ ̣] ̣ was printed, which was tentatively restored by Thomas 1978: 333 as φόρου ἀποτάκτου (cf. BL 7.27). Alpha may look acceptable at first sight, but, as far as I know, there are no parallels for such a reference to the rent on sheep. Upon closer inspection of the online image, the expected προβάτων can be read: what was taken as the belly of alpha is compatible with the right part of a pi (looped at the end as in l. 12), of which a high trace to the left would also survive. The loop of a small rho would be visible afterwards. A few further traces, inconclusive on their own, and an abraded area are followed by a long horizontal stroke, which fits well with the L-shaped symbol for ἔτους seen in P.Bour. 29.8. On this basis, I suggest reading φόρου π̣ρ̣ο̣β̣(άτων) [ιϛ] (ἔτους?).

As the text stands in the ed. pr., the two installments appear to have been paid through two different intermediaries (δι̣(ὰ) [Σώ]τ̣α Ἑρ̣ι̣έ̣ω̣ς̣ κο(ινωνοῦ), l. 6; διὰ Πεειοῦτ̣[ος] κ̣ο̣(ινωνοῦ), l. 11). The first intermediary would have been the same one who appears three years later in P.Bour. 29.7. However, the extant traces in l. 6 do not support the reading [Σώ]τ̣α Ἑρ̣ι̣έ̣ω̣ς̣, but rather seem consistent with [Π]ε̣ειεῦ̣τ̣ο̣ς, implying that the same intermediary made the payment on both occasions. (In l. 11, I read Πεειεῦτ̣[ος] instead of the ed. pr.’s Πεειοῦτ̣[ος].) The name Peeieus is not otherwise attested in this form, but, as already noted in BGU 13 2298.11 n., this person may be Paieus son of Stotoetis, known from several Soknopaiou Nesos papyri. To the occurrences listed in P.Messeri 30.3 n., showing various spellings of the name, add now P.Berl.Cohen 3 .4 (re-edited in Borrelli 2026: 231–233), from which we learn that he was an epiteretes in 195/6.
For another instance of a presbyteros who was previously appointed as an epiteretes, see e.g. SB 18 13143.5–9 (Philoteris, II).
